chunks.section: BMuon: Budgeting Muon’s Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility
chunks.text: Rida Assalouh rida.assalouh@polytechnique.edu Affiliation: Inria, Paris, France Affiliation: École polytechnique, Institut Polytechnique de Paris, Palaiseau, France Tom Jacobs tom.jacobs@cispa.de Affiliation: CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, Saarbrücken, Germany Rebekka Burkholz burkholz@cispa.de Affiliation: CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, Saarbrücken, Germany Yani Ioannou yani.ioannou@ucalgary.ca Affiliation: Schulich School of Engineering, University of Calgary, Calgary, Alberta, Canada Affiliation: Hotchkiss Brain Institute, University of Calgary, Calgary, Alberta, Canada Umut Şimşekli umut.simsekli@inria.fr Affiliation: Inria – Département d’Informatique de l’École Normale Supérieure, PSL Research University – CNRS, Paris, France

Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon’s optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon’s spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon’s geometry and structured sparse geometries. Our principal sparsity control is an interpretable global channel-allocation budget, rather than a setting-dependent sparsity-penalty coefficient. For linear factorization models, we show that Muon admits minimum-cost exact representations with redundant hidden width, whereas under the BMuon oracle geometry and a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost representation is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a minorization-maximization surrogate for the exact allocation problem. On ImageNet-1K with ViT-S/16, BMuon improves over Muon under gradual structured MLP pruning, and its learned allocations provide a more effective pruning criterion than weight magnitude. On a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves over Muon under post-training MLP channel pruning. Muon, steepest descent, spectral norm, structured pruning, structured sparsity, optimization geometry, Transformers

Modern Transformer models incur substantial memory and computational costs at inference time, motivating compression for more efficient deployment ( Kwon et al., 2022 ) . Pruning is a natural approach to this problem, but practical gains depend on the sparsity structure: unstructured sparsity often requires specialized kernels or hardware, whereas structured pruning removes entire computational units and translates directly into efficiency gains ( Wen et al., 2016 ; An et al., 2024 ) . Feed-forward modules can account for roughly two thirds of Transformer parameters ( Geva et al., 2021 ) , making their hidden channels a natural target for structured compression. Global pruning ranks channels across layers jointly, allowing different layers to retain different numbers of channels ( Lee et al., 2021 ; An et al., 2024 ) . Post-pruning fine-tuning adds computational cost, especially for large models ( Kwon et al., 2022 ; Sun et al., 2024 ) , motivating compressibility to emerge during training so that pruning requires little or no recovery. Figure 1 : Post-training global MLP pruning on ImageNet-1K with ViT-S/16. Mean ± \pm std over 3 seeds. See Appendix E.1 .

Muon has demonstrated strong training efficiency across model scales, from small vision and language-model benchmarks to billion-parameter language models ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Shah et al., 2025 ) . Its matrix update can be viewed as a linear minimization oracle over a spectral-norm ball, giving Muon a steepest-descent interpretation in spectral-norm geometry ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) . Prior work has shown that implicit bias can depend on optimization geometry ( Gunasekar et al., 2018 ) . For Muon, recent theory identifies a spectral-norm margin bias in linear and smooth homogeneous models ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Gronich and Vardi, 2026 ) . Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers degrade rapidly under structured MLP pruning, suggesting that Muon’s spectral geometry does not by itself encourage structured compressibility. As shown in Figure 1 , a Muon-trained ViT-S/16 on ImageNet-1K collapses after only 30 % 30\% global MLP channel pruning, with Top-1 accuracy falling from 75.23 % 75.23\% to 3.17 % 3.17\% . In contrast, our proposed Budget Muon (BMuon) algorithm retains 74.08 % 74.08\% Top-1 accuracy after 70 % 70\% pruning, nearly matching its 74.17 % 74.17\% accuracy before pruning, with no post-pruning recovery. This raises the central question: can Muon’s spectral geometry be modified to encourage structured compressibility?

To address this question, we introduce BMuon, which reweights Muon’s spectral geometry under a single global budget K K shared across all hidden channels of all MLP blocks. For hidden channel j j in block ℓ \ell , BMuon assigns an allocation μ j ℓ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \mu_{j}^{\ell}\in[0,1] to the corresponding row of the up-projection matrix and column of the down-projection matrix, with ∑ ℓ , j μ j ℓ = K \sum_{\ell,j}\mu_{j}^{\ell}=K . For a fixed allocation, BMuon introduces a diagonal reweighting inside Muon’s spectral-norm constraint, with the components of the update variable corresponding to channel j j in block ℓ \ell weighted according to its allocation μ j ℓ \mu_{j}^{\ell} . BMuon chooses the allocation globally, intuitively asking where the update budget should be spent to obtain the greatest first-order decrease in the loss.

NuMuon ( Dolatabadi et al., 2026 ) is the closest prior compression-aware variant of Muon. It imposes a nuclear-norm constraint on Muon’s update direction to improve low-rank compressibility. BMuon instead targets structured compressibility over hidden channels by introducing a global channel budget into Muon’s spectral-norm geometry. Prior work has also incorporated compressibility into training. Lu et al. (2022) train networks for unstructured pruning with Frank–Wolfe under fixed layerwise constraints on the weights, while Zimmer et al. (2025) use Frank–Wolfe under fixed norm constraints for convolutional filter pruning and low-rank compression. BMuon instead leaves the weights unconstrained and modifies Muon’s spectral update geometry for global hidden-channel compression. Resource-constrained structure learning and global structured pruning have been studied across CNNs and Transformers ( Gordon et al., 2018 ; Yu et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; An et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . GRASPrune ( Wang et al., 2026b ) learns gates post hoc on a frozen LLM to select MLP channels and attention KV-head groups under a single global parameter budget, while DABP ( Laroui et al., 2026 ) jointly trains CNN weights and continuous channel gates under a global resource budget. BMuon uses no forward gates; its budget instead controls the channel-wise reweighting of Muon’s spectral update constraint during training.

Theoretically, we show that the BMuon oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under an induced norm Ω α , K \Omega_{\alpha,K} , where α \alpha controls the strength of channel reweighting and K K is the global budget over the N N hidden channels. This family recovers Muon when α = 0 \alpha=0 or K = N K=N . At α = 1 \alpha=1 , its unit ball is the convex hull of operator-norm-bounded updates supported on at most K K coupled hidden channels. This is related to group k k -support norms through the use of structured support ( Argyriou et al., 2012 ; Rao et al., 2017 ) , but its atoms are bounded in operator norm rather than Euclidean norm. It is also related to spectral k k -support norms ( McDonald et al., 2014 ; McDonald et al., 2016 ) , but differs in the notion of sparsity: spectral k k -support uses sparsity in singular values, whereas BMuon uses MLP-channel sparsity. At α = K = 1 \alpha=K=1 , the norm reduces to an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} aggregation over coupled channel groups, yielding a group-lasso-like geometry ( Yuan and Lin, 2006 ) . We then characterize the representation cost induced by BMuon. Following Dai et al. (2021) , this is the minimum parameter-space cost among exact two-matrix factorizations that realize the same linear predictor. We prove that, under an explicit budget-scarcity condition, every minimum-cost BMuon factorization is width-minimal, whereas Muon’s minimum cost can also be attained by factorizations with redundant hidden width.

Solving the exact allocation problem at every training step is expensive. We therefore derive a minorization–maximization surrogate that yields a tractable allocation update, followed by the corresponding weighted Muon update. On CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K, BMuon outperforms Muon under both gradual and post-training global MLP-channel pruning, even when both use the same magnitude-based pruning criterion. Under gradual pruning, using the learned allocations themselves to rank channels further improves performance, showing that they also provide a useful measure of channel importance. The non-uniform architectures identified by BMuon in the gradual-pruning experiments also outperform matched uniform-width architectures when retrained from scratch, providing evidence that the learned allocation captures useful differences in how MLP capacity should be distributed across layers. Finally, on a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves robustness to post-training global MLP-channel pruning, showing that the effect extends to language modeling at substantially larger scale.

To summarize, our main contributions are: • We introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which incorporates a single global hidden-channel budget into Muon’s spectral update geometry, while coupling the matrix slices that define each MLP channel. • We characterize the induced norm family Ω α , K \Omega_{\alpha,K} and its relation to Muon and structured sparse geometries in Section 2 . In the linear factorization setting of Section 3 , we show that for a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost BMuon factorization is width-minimal, whereas Muon’s minimum cost is also attained by redundant-width factorizations. • We derive a practical minorization–maximization surrogate for the global allocation problem, yielding a tractable allocation update in Section 4 . • In Section 5 , we show across CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, and a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model that BMuon improves structured MLP-channel compressibility relative to Muon. In the vision experiments, the learned allocations also provide effective pruning scores and identify non-uniform MLP architectures that outperform matched uniform-width architectures when retrained from scratch.

Section 2 showed that the BMuon oracle performs steepest descent under Ω α , K \Omega_{\alpha,K} . We now ask whether minimizing Ω α , K \Omega_{\alpha,K} among parameterizations that realize the same predictor favors representations with fewer active hidden channels. This question is motivated by prior work showing that the norm underlying steepest descent can directly shape its implicit bias ( Gunasekar et al., 2018 ; Tsilivis et al., 2025 ; Fan et al., 2025 ; Jacobs et al., 2026 ) . Rather than establishing an implicit-bias result for BMuon, we characterize the exact parameterizations of a fixed predictor that minimize Ω α , K \Omega_{\alpha,K} , following the representation-cost view of Dai et al. (2021) ; Jagadeesan et al. (2022) . Each block realizes the matrix factorization W 2 ℓ ​ W 1 ℓ W_{2}^{\ell}W_{1}^{\ell} , corresponding to the setup in Eq. ( 1 ) with the identity activation and no bias. We first test whether BMuon produces models that can be compressed directly after training without post-compression fine-tuning. We train a small Vision Transformer on CIFAR-100 for 200 epochs over three seeds. We compare Muon, Muon with a proximal Group-Lasso penalty on coupled MLP channels (Muon+GL) ( Yuan and Lin, 2006 ; Wen et al., 2016 ) , NuMuon ( Dolatabadi et al., 2026 ) , and BMuon. NuMuon is particularly relevant as a direct comparison: it modifies the Muon update to improve compressibility, but targets low-rank structure through the singular spectrum, whereas BMuon targets structured MLP-channel compression. BMuon uses α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 and a budget annealed to 20 % 20\% of the total MLP-channel mass. Full experimental details in Appendix E.2 .

We restrict the compression to the ViT MLP blocks. Muon, Muon+GL, and BMuon are compressed by globally pruning hidden channels across all blocks. For magnitude-based pruning, channel j j in block ℓ \ell is ranked by s ℓ j = ∥ W ℓ 1 , j : ∥ 2 2 + ∥ W ℓ 2 , : , j ∥ 2 2 s^{\ell}_{j}=\sqrt{\|W^{\ell}_{1,j:}\|_{2}^{2}+\|W^{\ell}_{2,:,j}\|_{2}^{2}} . BMuon is pruned using both this score (BM-mag) and its final learned allocation μ \mu (BM- μ \mu ). NuMuon instead compresses each MLP weight matrix independently using truncated SVD, with ranks chosen to approximately match the parameter count of the corresponding channel-pruned model.

Figure 2 shows the post-training fragility that motivates this work: Muon falls to 5.72 % 5.72\% test accuracy after only 30 % 30\% MLP-channel pruning. Muon+GL remains robust through 50 % 50\% pruning, while NuMuon degrades more gradually under low-rank compression. Under magnitude-based pruning, BMuon is substantially more compressible than the structured baselines while matching Muon’s dense accuracy: BMuon reaches 71.46 % 71.46\% , versus 71.49 % 71.49\% for Muon, 71.25 % 71.25\% for Muon+GL, and 69.95 % 69.95\% for NuMuon. Using μ \mu for ranking provides a further gain: at 80 % 80\% pruning, BM- μ \mu retains 70.57 % 70.57\% accuracy, compared with 60.84 % 60.84\% for BM-mag, while Muon, Muon+GL, and NuMuon have fallen to 1.93 % 1.93\% , 6.01 % 6.01\% , and 3.84 % 3.84\% , respectively. The advantage of BM-mag under the shared magnitude criterion isolates the compressibility benefit of BMuon training, while the further gain from BM- μ \mu indicates that the learned allocation also carries useful channel-importance information.

We next ask whether BMuon’s compressibility advantage persists when channel pruning is interleaved with training and recovery ( Aketi et al., 2020 ) , and whether its learned allocation identifies useful architectures when retrained from scratch.

We evaluate gradual MLP-channel pruning during training from scratch on a ViT for CIFAR-100 and a ViT-S/16 for ImageNet-1K, targeting final pruning levels of 90 % 90\% and 95 % 95\% . All results are reported over three seeds. Each run starts dense and alternates between training and pruning. After each training phase, we rank all surviving MLP channels globally, permanently remove the lowest-ranked ones to reach the next sparsity target, and resume training from the surviving weights. We repeat this train–prune cycle until the final pruning level is reached, and then continue training for recovery. We compare three methods. Muon-mag trains with Muon and ranks channels by the coupled weight-magnitude score introduced in Section 5.1 . BMuon-mag trains the MLPs with BMuon ( α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 ) and uses the same magnitude ranking. BMuon- μ \mu uses the same BMuon training but ranks channels by the learned allocation μ \mu . During each BMuon training phase, the global budget is annealed to the next target channel count over the first half of the phase and held fixed for the second half. As an additional control, we test whether the architecture selected by BMuon- μ \mu is useful on its own. We keep only its final per-block widths, initialize a new model with those widths, and train it from scratch with standard Muon for the same training horizon. As a baseline, we also train a uniform-width model from scratch with nearly the same total number of MLP channels. Full details are given in Appendix E.4 .

On the unpruned models, Muon achieves lower perplexity ( 10.92 10.92 versus 12.84 12.84 for BMuon), but its performance degrades rapidly under pruning. In contrast, BMuon preserves its unpruned performance up to 80 % 80\% pruning, reaching 12.86 12.86 with activation ranking and 12.85 12.85 with μ \mu ranking. BMuon substantially outperforms Muon when both use the same magnitude or activation criterion at moderate and high pruning levels, while μ \mu again provides an effective pruning score. Overall, BMuon trades some unpruned quality for substantially greater robustness to structured channel pruning.

Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply under post-training MLP-channel pruning, motivating the question of whether Muon’s spectral geometry can be modified to favor structured compressibility. BMuon addresses this question by reweighting hidden channels within Muon’s spectral-norm constraints and making them compete for a global budget. We show that the resulting norm family recovers Muon and connects it to channel-sparse geometries. In linear two-factor models, Muon admits minimum-cost factorizations with redundant hidden width, whereas under a sufficiently scarce BMuon budget every minimum-cost factorization is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a tractable minorization–maximization approximation to the global allocation oracle. Across vision and language models, BMuon is substantially more robust than Muon to magnitude-based MLP-channel pruning. The learned allocation also provides an effective pruning score and identifies useful non-uniform MLP architectures when retrained from scratch. Several questions remain open. Our theoretical results characterize representation cost in linear two-factor models; studying the implicit bias of BMuon training, particularly beyond the linear setting, is an important direction for future work. Another direction is to design a practical BMuon algorithm with provable approximation guarantees to the oracle. Our experiments focus on MLP hidden channels, and extending the global budget to other structured components of Transformers remains to be explored. Finally, BMuon can trade dense-model quality for greater pruning robustness, as observed in our language-model experiments; characterizing this tradeoff at larger model scales is a natural direction for future work.

This appendix provides the derivations and proofs underlying the MM allocation update of Section 4 . Appendix D.1 proves the tight minorization in Eq. ( 7 ) and establishes the sign properties of the allocation scores a j ℓ a_{j}^{\ell} . Appendix D.2 solves the surrogate maximization problem and derives the closed-form update in Eq. ( 8 ), including the determination of λ μ \lambda_{\mu} by bisection. Appendix D.3 proves monotonicity of repeated MM updates and, for 0 < α ≤ 1 2 0<\alpha\leq\tfrac{1}{2} , convergence in objective value to the global optimum over 𝒦 K , ε \mathcal{K}_{K,\varepsilon} together with global optimality of every accumulation point. chunks.section: D.5 Approximation of the allocation oracle
chunks.text: As in Algorithm 1 , BMuon does not recompute the allocation μ \mu at every optimizer step. Instead, every five optimizer steps it performs an allocation refresh : μ \mu is recomputed and then kept fixed for the next four optimizer steps. The budget may be scheduled over training, so we write K t K_{t} for the budget at optimizer step t t . At a refresh step t t , the new allocation is computed under the current budget K t K_{t} . The practical implementation therefore introduces two approximations. First, at each allocation refresh, we perform only one MM update instead of solving the allocation problem to convergence. Second, we refresh μ \mu only once every five optimizer steps, rather than at every optimizer step. We measure these two errors separately, and then test whether replacing the practical one-step update by a certified solve at each refresh changes the training and compression results.

We use the same CIFAR-100 ViT and training setup as in Appendix E.2 , except that we train for 100 epochs. As in our training experiments, we use α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 . For each seed, we run two paired versions of BMuon that differ only in how the allocation μ \mu is computed at an allocation refresh. The MLPs contain N = 4608 N=4608 hidden channels in total. The budget K t K_{t} decreases linearly from N N to 0.3 ​ N 0.3N during the first third of training and is then kept fixed. In this experiment, K t K_{t} changes only at allocation refreshes, so it is constant during the four intervening optimizer steps. In both runs, μ \mu is refreshed every five optimizer steps and is held fixed between two consecutive refreshes. The two runs differ only in how μ \mu is computed at a refresh step t t . In the 1-step refresh run , we start from the allocation carried from the previous refresh, compute the MM scores using NS 5 \mathrm{NS}_{5} , the five-step Newton–Schulz approximation defined in Appendix A , and perform one MM update under the current budget K t K_{t} . In the certified refresh run , we instead use exact polar factors and repeat the MM update until the stopping condition Eq. ( 25 ) is satisfied. In both runs, the allocation computed at step t t satisfies the current constraint ∑ i μ i = K t \sum_{i}\mu_{i}=K_{t} . Apart from this difference, the two runs use the same BMuon weight update. For each seed, they also use the same initialization, data order, augmentation stream, and budget schedule.

The previous experiments measure the approximation error in the allocation objective. We now test whether this error changes the trained model. Figure 5 compares the two runs. For each model, we rank all MLP channels globally by the corresponding entries of its final allocation μ \mu and remove those with the smallest values. Both runs refresh μ \mu every five optimizer steps. Thus, the end-to-end comparison isolates the difference between one practical MM update and the certified allocation μ t ref \mu_{t}^{\mathrm{ref}} at each refresh; it does not compare against a run that recomputes a certified allocation at every optimizer step. Figure 4 (b) separately shows that keeping μ \mu fixed during the four intervening steps introduces only a small objective error at the sampled states.

Relative to Muon, BMuon’s additional computation is confined to the budgeted matrices (the MLP weights; Algorithm 1 ); all other parameters are updated exactly as in Muon. On steps where the allocation is not updated, BMuon uses the same number of Newton–Schulz polar evaluations as Muon, with only additional channelwise row/column scalings by D μ α D_{\mu}^{\alpha} . On an allocation-update step, BMuon performs one additional polar evaluation per budgeted matrix to construct the MM surrogate, before recomputing the weighted polar factor used for the parameter update. Updating the allocation every Δ ​ T μ \Delta T_{\mu} steps therefore raises the amortized number of polar evaluations per budgeted matrix from 1 1 to 1 + 1 / Δ ​ T μ 1+1/\Delta T_{\mu} per optimizer step, i.e. 1.2 1.2 for Δ ​ T μ = 5 \Delta T_{\mu}=5 . Once the surrogate polar factors are available, the channel scores require only row/column inner products, and the allocation update consists of channelwise operations and a scalar bisection over the global budget. The only persistent additional optimizer state is the allocation vector μ ∈ ℝ N \mu\in\mathbb{R}^{N} , one scalar per budgeted channel, which is negligible next to the momentum buffers. We verify empirically that this overhead is small in practice by comparing end-to-end training times against Muon at the allocation-update frequency used throughout our experiments, Δ ​ T μ = 5 \Delta T_{\mu}=5 , on the ImageNet-1K ViT-S/16 and 1B-parameter LLaMA settings of Appendices E.4 and E.5 . All measurements use eight H100 GPUs and the same Muon and BMuon implementations as the corresponding training runs.

This section provides the experimental details and additional results for Section 5 . Appendix E.1 gives the ImageNet-1K post-training pruning setup and full pruning results. Appendix E.2 gives the CIFAR-100 post-training compression setup and full pruning results. Appendix E.3 studies the effect of the global budget K K . We use a custom PyTorch ViT-S/16 implementation following the plain-ViT design of Beyer et al. (2022) : 224 × 224 224\times 224 inputs, 16 × 16 16\times 16 patches, embedding dimension 384 384 , 12 Transformer blocks, six attention heads, MLP width 1536 1536 , fixed two-dimensional sinusoidal positional embeddings, global average pooling over patch tokens, and a pre-logits representation layer. The model therefore contains 12 × 1536 = 18,432 12\times 1536=18{,}432 MLP hidden channels. Our ImageNet-1K optimization setup follows the ViT-S/16 configuration of Zhong et al. (2026) . Matrix-valued parameters within the Transformer blocks are optimized with Muon, while the remaining parameters are optimized with AdamW. We use global batch size 4096 4096 , Muon learning rate 3 ​ 3 × 10 − 3 3\sqrt{3}\times 10^{-3} , AdamW learning rate 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , weight decay 0.3 0.3 , Muon momentum 0.95 0.95 with Nesterov, and dropout 0.1 0.1 . Training uses sigmoid binary cross entropy with label smoothing 0.1 0.1 , random resized crops, and horizontal flips, without Mixup, CutMix, RandAugment, random erasing, or stochastic depth. Muon uses five Newton–Schulz iterations following Jordan et al. (2024) and the Moonlight-style RMS-matching scale 0.2 ​ max ⁡ ( d out , d in ) 0.2\sqrt{\max(d_{\mathrm{out}},d_{\mathrm{in}})} ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . All models are trained for 150 epochs with 5000 warmup steps followed by cosine learning-rate decay to zero, using a half-length adaptation of the 300-epoch, 10,000-step ViT-S/16 schedule of Zhong et al. (2026) .

BMuon is applied only to the MLP matrices; the remaining Muon-eligible Transformer matrices use ordinary Muon. We use α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 , one MM allocation update every five optimizer steps, and ε = 10 − 6 \varepsilon=10^{-6} . Let N = 18,432 N=18{,}432 denote the total number of MLP hidden channels. The global allocation budget is initialized at K ⁡ ( 0 ) = N K(0)=N and linearly annealed to K target = 5,530 ≈ 0.30 ​ N K_{\mathrm{target}}=5{,}530\approx 0.30N during the first 25 % 25\% of training, after which it is held fixed for the remaining 75 % 75\% .

After training, we take the final epoch-150 checkpoint and perform one-shot global structured pruning of coupled MLP hidden channels. Each pruning level is evaluated independently from the same dense checkpoint; pruning is therefore not cumulative, and no post-pruning fine-tuning or recovery is performed. All 18,432 18{,}432 channels are ranked jointly across the 12 blocks, subject to a minimum of four surviving channels per block. At 50 % 50\% MLP-channel pruning, these settings retain 9.71 % 9.71\% , 16.30 % 16.30\% , and 71.25 % 71.25\% test accuracy, respectively. We therefore use λ GL = 0.05 \lambda_{\mathrm{GL}}=0.05 throughout this experiment.

NuMuon ( Dolatabadi et al., 2026 ) is applied during training to all Muon-eligible Transformer weight matrices: the fused QKV projection, attention output projection, and the two MLP projections in each of the six blocks, for 24 matrices in total. Following the authors’ cosine rank-scheduling strategy, we use a 10 % 10\% initial full-rank period and, in our implementation, cosine-anneal the relative update rank from 1.0 1.0 to 0.25 0.25 between 10 % 10\% and 80 % 80\% of training, holding it at 0.25 0.25 thereafter. Since all eligible matrices have q = min ⁡ ( d in , d out ) = 192 q=\min(d_{\mathrm{in}},d_{\mathrm{out}})=192 , this corresponds to a final update rank of 48 48 . Full-rank steps use the standard Newton–Schulz Muon update, while reduced-rank steps use randomized Block Krylov with two Krylov iterations. The NuMuon paper reports an oversampling setting of 8 8 ; in our implementation, we realize this as a Krylov working dimension b = min ⁡ ( q , k + 8 ) b=\min(q,k+8) , where k = ⌈ r ⁡ ( t ) ​ q ⌉ k=\lceil r(t)q\rceil is the target update rank.

Compression is restricted to the ViT MLP blocks. We evaluate compression ratios { 0 , 0.1 , … , 0.9 , 0.95 } \{0,0.1,\ldots,0.9,0.95\} independently from the same final checkpoint, without cumulative pruning or post-compression fine-tuning. Muon, Muon+GL, and BMuon use global hidden-channel pruning over all six blocks. Magnitude pruning ranks channel j j in block ℓ \ell by s j ℓ = ∥ W ℓ 1 , j : ∥ 2 2 + ∥ W ℓ 2 , : , j ∥ 2 2 s_{j}^{\ell}=\sqrt{\|W^{\ell}_{1,j:}\|_{2}^{2}+\|W^{\ell}_{2,:,j}\|_{2}^{2}} . BMuon is evaluated with both this ranking and its final learned allocation μ \mu . During global pruning, we skip any candidate removal that would leave an MLP block with fewer than four hidden channels.

At evaluation, NuMuon compresses only the 12 MLP weight matrices using truncated SVD; attention weights remain dense. We distribute the retained rank budget as evenly as possible across matrices, with minimum rank 4. At each compression level, we choose the NuMuon rank so that the resulting whole-model parameter count is as close as possible to that of the corresponding structured-pruned model. Table 5 reports the exact post-training compression results corresponding to Fig. 2 . Table 5 : CIFAR-100 post-training compression results. Test accuracy (%) reported as mean ± \pm sample standard deviation over three seeds. All compression levels are evaluated independently from the final epoch-200 checkpoint, without post-compression fine-tuning.

chunks.section: E.3 Effect of the Global Budget
chunks.text: We ablate the global budget K K on the CIFAR-100 post-training compression setup of Appendix E.2 .

We use the same six-block ViT, 200-epoch training recipe, and optimization settings as in Appendix E.2 . We train BMuon with α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 and K / N ∈ { 0.1 , 0.2 , … , 0.9 } , K/N\in\{0.1,0.2,\ldots,0.9\}, with no budget schedule and holding all other hyperparameters fixed. After training, we perform global MLP-channel pruning without recovery, ranking channels either by coupled weight magnitude, s j ℓ = ∥ W ℓ 1 , j : ∥ 2 2 + ∥ W ℓ 2 , : , j ∥ 2 2 , s_{j}^{\ell}=\sqrt{\|W^{\ell}_{1,j:}\|_{2}^{2}+\|W^{\ell}_{2,:,j}\|_{2}^{2}}, or by the final learned allocation μ \mu . (a) Magnitude ranking. (b) μ \mu ranking. Figure 6 : Effect of the budget on post-training compression. CIFAR-100 test accuracy after global MLP-channel pruning for different budget ratios K / N K/N . Panel (a) uses coupled weight-magnitude ranking, while panel (b) uses the final learned allocation μ \mu . Mean ± \pm sample std. over three seeds. Figure 6 shows that the budget directly controls the compression level favored during training. With magnitude pruning, models remain robust approximately up to pruning a fraction 1 − K / N 1-K/N of the channels, and degrade sharply beyond this point. The same pattern holds with μ \mu ranking, but the degradation is generally more gradual, further showing that μ \mu provides a useful channel-importance signal. For the most restrictive budgets, particularly K / N = 0.1 K/N=0.1 and 0.2 0.2 , the accuracy of the unpruned model also decreases slightly, indicating a tradeoff between aggressive compressibility and performance before pruning.

All gradual-pruning experiments use seeds 0 , 1 , 2 0,1,2 . Only MLP hidden channels are pruned, and all surviving channels are ranked globally across blocks at each pruning event. We enforce at least four surviving channels per block. Muon-mag and BMuon-mag use the coupled magnitude score s j ℓ = ∥ W ℓ 1 , j : ∥ 2 2 + ∥ W ℓ 2 , : , j ∥ 2 2 s_{j}^{\ell}=\sqrt{\|W^{\ell}_{1,j:}\|_{2}^{2}+\|W^{\ell}_{2,:,j}\|_{2}^{2}} , while BMuon- μ \mu uses s j ℓ , μ = μ j ℓ s_{j}^{\ell,\mu}=\mu_{j}^{\ell} . After pruning, training resumes from the surviving weights and optimizer state; pruned channels never return.

On both CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K, BMuon is applied only to the MLP matrices, with α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 , one MM step every five optimizer steps, and ε = 10 − 6 \varepsilon=10^{-6} . At the start of each training phase i i , let N start , i N_{\mathrm{start},i} denote the current number of surviving channels and let N end , i N_{\mathrm{end},i} denote the number of channels to retain at the next pruning event. During the first half of phase i i , the BMuon budget is linearly annealed from N start , i N_{\mathrm{start},i} to N end , i N_{\mathrm{end},i} ; during the second half, it is held fixed at N end , i N_{\mathrm{end},i} . At the end of the phase, pruning reduces the network to exactly N end , i N_{\mathrm{end},i} surviving channels. After pruning, the allocation coordinates μ \mu of all surviving channels are reset to one.

We use a six-block ViT with 32 × 32 32\times 32 inputs, 4 × 4 4\times 4 patches, embedding dimension 112 112 , four attention heads, and MLP width 448 448 , giving 2688 2688 prunable channels. Training lasts 200 epochs with batch size 256. Muon uses learning rate 0.02 0.02 , momentum 0.95 0.95 without Nesterov, weight decay 0.05 0.05 , and five Newton–Schulz steps; auxiliary parameters use AdamW with learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} and weight decay 0.05 0.05 . We use five epochs of linear warmup followed by cosine decay to 1 % 1\% of the initial learning rate. Training uses random cropping and horizontal flipping, RandAugment ( 2 , 9 ) (2,9) , random erasing with probability 0.1 0.1 , and Mixup/CutMix with parameters 0.8 / 1.0 0.8/1.0 and total probability 0.5 0.5 . For the 90 % 90\% experiment, cumulative pruning levels of 20 , 40 , 60 , 75 , 85 , 20,40,60,75,85, and 90 % 90\% are applied after epochs 30 , 60 , 90 , 120 , 150 , 30,60,90,120,150, and 180 180 , respectively, followed by 20 recovery epochs. The corresponding surviving channel counts are 2150 , 1613 , 1075 , 672 , 403 , 2150,1613,1075,672,403, and 269 269 . For the 95 % 95\% experiment, cumulative pruning levels of 20 , 40 , 60 , 75 , 85 , 90 , 20,40,60,75,85,90, and 95 % 95\% are applied after epochs 26 , 52 , 78 , 104 , 130 , 155 , 26,52,78,104,130,155, and 180 180 , respectively, followed by 20 recovery epochs. The corresponding surviving channel counts are 2150 , 1613 , 1075 , 672 , 403 , 269 , 2150,1613,1075,672,403,269, and 134 134 .

We use the same ViT-S/16 architecture, ImageNet-1K data pipeline, base optimizer hyperparameters, and 150-epoch learning-rate schedule as in Appendix E.1 . Unlike the post-training pruning experiment, here physical MLP-channel removal is interleaved with training according to the gradual-pruning protocol described above. For the 90 % 90\% experiment, cumulative pruning levels of 20 , 40 , 60 , 70 , 80 , 20,40,60,70,80, and 90 % 90\% are applied after epochs 22 , 44 , 66 , 87 , 108 , 22,44,66,87,108, and 129 129 , respectively, followed by 21 recovery epochs. The corresponding surviving channel counts are 14,746 , 11 , 059 , 7 , 373 , 5 , 530 , 3 , 686 , 14{,}746,11{,}059,7{,}373,5{,}530,3{,}686, and 1,843 1{,}843 . For the 95 % 95\% experiment, cumulative pruning levels of 20 , 40 , 60 , 70 , 80 , 90 , 20,40,60,70,80,90, and 95 % 95\% are applied after epochs 19 , 38 , 57 , 76 , 95 , 114 , 19,38,57,76,95,114, and 132 132 , respectively, followed by 18 recovery epochs. The corresponding surviving channel counts are 14,746, 11,059, 7,373, 5,530, 3,686, 1,843, and 922.

For CIFAR-100, we report final Top-1 accuracy on the test set at epoch 200. For ImageNet-1K, we report final Top-1 accuracy on the full 50,000-image validation set at epoch 150. In both cases, evaluation is performed after the final recovery stage. Reported means and standard deviations are over seeds 0 , 1 , 2 0,1,2 .

For each BMuon- μ \mu pruning run, we record the final per-block MLP widths. To evaluate the selected architecture on its own, we instantiate a new model with these widths and train it from scratch with standard Muon, without pruning, using the same training recipe and horizon. As a baseline, we also train a uniform-width model from scratch with standard Muon, with its total MLP channel count matched as closely as possible to the corresponding architecture discovered by BMuon- μ \mu . Seed pairing is one-to-one: the architecture discovered with seed i i is retrained from scratch using seed i i . Thus, for seeds 0 , 1 , 2 0,1,2 , we perform three retraining runs rather than a 3 × 3 3\times 3 crossing of discovery and retraining seeds. Our LLaMA/FineWeb experiments are based on the LLaMA-1B setup of Muon+ ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) 1 1 1 https://github.com/K1seki221/MuonPlus . We adopt its architecture and training recipe, reducing only the number of Transformer blocks from 24 24 to 17 17 to obtain a 986,746,880 986{,}746{,}880 -parameter model; all other architectural hyperparameters are unchanged. The Muon+ codebase builds on Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) and the modded-nanogpt training framework 2 2 2 https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt . We retain its LLaMA-2 tokenizer and FineWeb preprocessing and sharding conventions, Muon parameter routing, auxiliary AdamW-style updates for non-Muon parameters, momentum/Nesterov convention, five-step Newton–Schulz polar approximation, matrix learning-rate shape/RMS scaling, warmup–cosine schedule, and BF16 training conventions. For our experiments, we integrate BMuon into the SwiGLU MLPs.

We use a 17-layer pre-norm LLaMA-style causal decoder with hidden dimension 2048 2048 , 32 32 attention and 32 32 key–value heads, SwiGLU width 5461 5461 , context length 4096 4096 , vocabulary size 32,000 32{,}000 , RMSNorm ( ϵ = 10 − 5 \epsilon=10^{-5} ), and RoPE with θ = 10,000 \theta=10{,}000 . The token embedding and language-model head are untied. The model has 986,746,880 986{,}746{,}880 parameters. Each SwiGLU layer contains gate, up, and down projections W g , W u ∈ ℝ 5461 × 2048 W_{g},W_{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{5461\times 2048} and W d ∈ ℝ 2048 × 5461 W_{d}\in\mathbb{R}^{2048\times 5461} , giving N = 17 × 5461 = 92,837 N=17\times 5461=92{,}837 structural MLP channels in total. We train on 13,090,422,784 13{,}090{,}422{,}784 tokens from the sample-100BT configuration of FineWeb, using the LLaMA-2 tokenizer.

Training uses BF16 with an effective global batch of 512 512 sequences, corresponding to 2,097,152 2{,}097{,}152 tokens per optimizer step. We use seeds { 0 , 1 , 2 } \{0,1,2\} for all methods. For Muon matrices, we use learning rate 0.02 0.02 , momentum 0.95 0.95 with Nesterov momentum, five Newton–Schulz iterations, decoupled weight decay 0.1 0.1 , gradient clipping at 1.0 1.0 , a 10 % 10\% linear warmup, and cosine decay to zero. Embeddings, normalization parameters, and the language-model head use the auxiliary AdamW-style branch with β 1 = β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=0.95 and ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} . In the Muon baseline, attention and MLP matrices use Muon. For BMuon, the three SwiGLU projection matrices in each block are instead updated by BMuon, while attention matrices continue to use standard Muon.

We use α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 and a budget K = 18,567 ≈ 0.2 ​ N K=18{,}567\approx 0.2N throughout training, with no budget schedule. The allocation is updated every five optimizer steps with one MM iteration, using a numerical floor ϵ = 10 − 6 \epsilon=10^{-6} .

We prune only SwiGLU hidden channels. Pruning channel j j in layer ℓ \ell jointly removes W g ℓ [ j , : ] W_{g}^{\ell}[j,:] , W u ℓ [ j , : ] W_{u}^{\ell}[j,:] , and W d ℓ [ : , j ] W_{d}^{\ell}[:,j] . For each pruning ratio r ∈ { 0 , 0.1 , … , 0.9 } r\in\{0,0.1,\ldots,0.9\} , we restore the unpruned checkpoint and prune directly to ratio r r . Scores are ranked globally across all Transformer blocks, with a minimum of 10 surviving channels per layer. For both Muon and BMuon, the magnitude score is s ℓ ​ j mag = ( ∥ W g ℓ [ j , : ] ∥ 2 2 + ∥ W u ℓ [ j , : ] ∥ 2 2 + ∥ W d ℓ [ : , j ] ∥ 2 2 ) 1 / 2 . s_{\ell j}^{\mathrm{mag}}=\left(\|W_{g}^{\ell}[j,:]\|_{2}^{2}+\|W_{u}^{\ell}[j,:]\|_{2}^{2}+\|W_{d}^{\ell}[:,j]\|_{2}^{2}\right)^{1/2}. For BMuon, we additionally use s ℓ ​ j μ = μ j ℓ . s_{\ell j}^{\mu}=\mu_{j}^{\ell}. For the activation-aware criterion, let h ℓ ​ j ( x ) = SiLU ( W g ℓ [ j , : ] x ) ( W u ℓ [ j , : ] x ) h_{\ell j}(x)=\operatorname{SiLU}\!\left(W_{g}^{\ell}[j,:]x\right)\left(W_{u}^{\ell}[j,:]x\right) denote the hidden activation of channel j j . We score it by s ℓ ​ j act = 𝔼 x ​ [ h ℓ ​ j ​ ( x ) 2 ] ∥ W d ℓ [ : , j ] ∥ 2 . s_{\ell j}^{\mathrm{act}}=\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{x}[h_{\ell j}(x)^{2}]}\,\|W_{d}^{\ell}[:,j]\|_{2}. Activation statistics are accumulated in FP32 over 1,048,576 1{,}048{,}576 calibration tokens. Each pruned model is evaluated without recovery on 5,046,272 5{,}046{,}272 validation tokens. Entries report mean ± \pm sample std. over seeds { 0 , 1 , 2 } \{0,1,2\} . No post-pruning recovery is performed.
